objectives: Describe how a message travels between two computers as packets
Explain the roles of IP addresses, ports and routers
Tell a client from a server

exercises.prompt: Explain in your own words why the internet splits messages into packets and what TCP adds.
exercises.answer: Packets let a lost piece be resent without resending the whole message, and let them take different routes. IP just delivers packets on a best-effort basis. TCP numbers them, confirms what arrived, resends missing ones and puts them back in order.

exercises.prompt: A server at 203.0.113.5 runs a website on port 443 and a database on port 5432. What does each part of 203.0.113.5:443 identify?
exercises.answer: The IP address identifies the computer on the network. The port identifies the program on that computer that should receive the data, here the web server instead of the database.

practical.title: Watch the hops
practical.task: Run ping and then tracert (Windows) or traceroute against a website you use. Note how many routers the packets pass and how the time changes.
practical.done: You can explain what each hop is and why times vary.

objectives: Name the parts of a URL
Walk through a DNS lookup step by step
Explain how caching and TTL affect DNS changes

exercises.answer: Scheme https, host api.example.com, port 8443, path /v1/items, query limit=5, fragment top. The fragment stays in the browser and is not sent to the server.

exercises.prompt: Describe the DNS lookup for www.example.com when no cache has the answer.
exercises.answer: The recursive resolver asks a root server, which points to the .com servers. A .com server points to example.com's authoritative server, which returns the IP address. The resolver caches it for the TTL and returns it to the client.

practical.title: Look up a name
practical.task: Run nslookup or dig for a domain you use. Find the A record and its TTL, then run it again and see whether the TTL goes down.
practical.done: You can point at the IP address and the TTL and say what they mean.

objectives: Read a raw HTTP request and response
Pick a method and a status code that fit a situation
Say what headers and the body are for

exercises.prompt: Write the raw HTTP request that fetches /about from www.example.com.
exercises.answer: GET /about HTTP/1.1, then a Host: www.example.com header, then a blank line. GET has no body, so the request ends after the headers.

exercises.prompt: A client sends a valid request to create an order, and the server saves it. Then another client requests an order that does not exist. Which status codes fit?
exercises.answer: 201 Created for the saved order, and 404 Not Found for the missing one. Both are chosen by what happened: success is 2xx and a client asking for something absent is 4xx.

practical.title: Read a real response
practical.task: Run curl -i against a website, then read the status line, the headers and where the body starts. Try a path that does not exist.
practical.done: You can name the status line, two headers and the body in the output.

objectives: Choose methods and status codes by their semantics
Use conditional requests
Explain what HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 change

exercises.prompt: What's the difference between 401 and 403? Between PUT and PATCH with respect to idempotency?
exercises.answer: 401 means the caller isn't authenticated, or the credentials are invalid. 403 means the server knows who you are but refuses. PUT replaces the resource and is idempotent by definition. PATCH applies changes and isn't guaranteed to be idempotent: an "increment by one" patch applied twice gives a different result.

exercises.prompt: Explain how ETag and If-None-Match work together. How would If-Match prevent a lost update in an API?
exercises.answer: The server returns an ETag. The client sends it back in If-None-Match, and if it's unchanged the server replies 304 with no body, saving bandwidth. If-Match on a PUT says to apply this only if the resource still has that version. Otherwise the server returns 412, so the client refetches rather than overwriting someone else's change.

practical.title: Add optimistic concurrency to an API
practical.task: Add ETag and If-Match to one resource in a small API. Return 412 on a stale write and 428 if the header is missing. Test it with two clients using curl.
practical.done: The second client's stale write is rejected, and it succeeds after refetching.

objectives: Explain what CORS does and doesn't protect
Predict when a request triggers a preflight
Set Cache-Control correctly for a single-page app

exercises.prompt: Your API returns a CORS error in the browser, but the same request works in curl. Why? Does CORS protect your API from attackers?
exercises.answer: CORS is enforced by the browser, which blocks the page from reading a cross-origin response unless the server allows it. curl doesn't enforce it. It protects users' browser sessions from other websites, not your API. Anyone can still call the API directly, so authentication and authorisation must live on the server.

exercises.prompt: After a deploy, some users of your single-page app see a blank page until they hard refresh. What's the likely cause, and what caching rules fix it?
exercises.answer: index.html was cached and still references hashed bundles that the deploy has removed, so those requests fail. Serve index.html with Cache-Control: no-cache so it's revalidated each time, serve hashed assets with a long max-age and immutable, and keep old assets available for a while after a deploy.

practical.title: Debug a preflight
practical.task: Serve a page and an API on different local ports. Call the API with a custom header and watch the OPTIONS request in DevTools. Make it fail, then fix it by setting the right response headers.
practical.done: You can say which header triggered the preflight and which response header fixed it.

objectives: Explain why logging in needs cookies or tokens
Compare sessions and signed tokens
Name the basic rules for storing passwords and cookies safely

exercises.prompt: Trace a session-cookie login from the password check to the next request.
exercises.answer: The client POSTs the credentials, and the server checks them and creates a session record. It replies with Set-Cookie holding a random session ID. The browser sends that cookie on later requests, and the server looks up the ID to find the user.

exercises.prompt: Compare a server-side session with a JWT for a mobile app. When would you pick each?
exercises.answer: Sessions are easy to revoke but need server storage. JWTs need no lookup and suit APIs and many services, but are hard to revoke, so they must be short-lived. Choose sessions when instant logout matters and tokens when stateless scaling matters.

practical.title: Watch a login
practical.task: Log in to a site you use with DevTools open on the Network tab. Find the login request, the Set-Cookie header and the Cookie header on a later request.
practical.done: You can show where the session ID is set and sent.

objectives: Trace what happens before the first HTTP byte
Plan a DNS migration around TTLs
Diagnose production bugs caused by TCP behaviour

exercises.prompt: List the steps and round trips before the first HTTP byte on a new HTTPS connection over TCP with TLS 1.3. What can reduce them?
exercises.answer: DNS lookup, TCP handshake (one round trip), TLS 1.3 handshake (one round trip), and then the request. Connection reuse removes the handshakes, TLS session resumption shortens the TLS step, and HTTP/3 over QUIC combines the transport and TLS handshakes.

exercises.prompt: You must move a service to a new IP address with a DNS record whose TTL is 24 hours. How do you do it safely?
exercises.answer: Lower the TTL at least 24 hours in advance, so the old value expires from caches. Then switch the record, keep the old address serving until traffic stops (some clients ignore TTLs), and raise the TTL again afterwards.

practical.title: Time a real request
practical.task: Use curl -w with time_namelookup, time_connect, time_appconnect and time_starttransfer against a site you use. Run it twice, and try a second request on a reused connection.
practical.done: You can say how much of the total was DNS, TCP, TLS and server time, and what reuse saved.

objectives: Set cookie attributes and say what each one prevents
Prevent XSS and CSRF
Weigh the options for storing tokens in a single-page app

exercises.prompt: What do HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite each protect against? Which of these stops CSRF?
exercises.answer: HttpOnly keeps JavaScript from reading the cookie, which limits session theft through XSS. Secure sends it only over HTTPS. SameSite stops the browser attaching it to cross-site requests, which is the one that defends against CSRF, usually alongside CSRF tokens. None of them stops an XSS script from making requests as the user.

exercises.prompt: Your single-page app keeps a JWT in localStorage. What's the risk, what's the common alternative, and what does that alternative cost you?
exercises.answer: Any XSS can read the token and use it elsewhere until it expires. A common alternative is a short-lived access token in memory, plus a refresh token in an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie, or a backend-for-frontend holding tokens on the server. Cookies then bring CSRF back into scope, and the design is more complex.

practical.title: Test your own app
practical.task: On a local app you own, check cookie attributes in DevTools, try a stored XSS payload in a text field, and add a Content-Security-Policy in report-only mode. Only test systems you own.
practical.done: You have a short list of what you found and what you changed, and you've read the CSP reports.
